query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying multi-step thermomechanical treatment (e.g., controlled forging and annealing) to high-entropy alloys will stabilize targeted phases, refine microstructure, and optimize mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized high-entropy alloy in a near-equiatomic composition before any thermomechanical processing
generation.intervention: Systematic multi-step forging (modulating temperature and strain rate) followed by carefully controlled annealing cycles
generation.conditions: Forging at elevated temperatures sufficient to induce plastic flow, with modest strain rates and cooling paths designed to manage recrystallization kinetics
generation.structural_mediator: Refinement of microstructure through dynamic recrystallization and controlled phase transformations
generation.mechanism: Deformation and subsequent thermal exposure promote dislocation generation and annihilation in a controlled manner, facilitating grain boundary formation, stabilizing desired phases, and increasing strength without a commensurate loss in ductility
generation.predicted_outcome: Higher strength and ductility relative to as-cast or single-step thermally treated microstructures
generation.baseline: Material processed by a single pass or direct annealing with relatively coarse grains and less optimal mechanical properties
generation.boundary: Overly high forging or annealing temperatures and inadequate strain rates can lead to excessive grain coarsening or unwanted phase formation, reversing benefits
generation.uncertainty: Exact gains in strength or ductility vary with alloy composition and specific processing parameters, thus requiring further validation

falsification_experiment.design: Compare three sets of samples: (1) no thermomechanical treatment, (2) single-step forging and annealing, and (3) multi-step forging with intermediate temperature holds and controlled cooling. Conduct standardized mechanical testing and microstructural analysis to quantify improvements.
measurements: Electron microscopy for grain size and phase distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If multi-step thermomechanical processing fails to measurably enhance phase stability, reduce grain size, or improve mechanical properties compared to non- or single-step processed samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
